contract_plain_english: If X and Y are any two jointly defined sub-gaussian real random variables—even dependent and not centered—then their product XY is sub-exponential and satisfies the exact bound ∥XY∥ψ1 ≤ ∥X∥ψ2 ∥Y∥ψ2.

source_evidence.observation: The lemma states: let X and Y be sub-gaussian random variables; then XY is sub-exponential, and ∥XY∥ψ1 ≤ ∥X∥ψ2 ∥Y∥ψ2.

source_evidence.anchor: Proof of Lemma 2.7.7, normalization and display (2.22)
source_evidence.observation: The proof normalizes ∥X∥ψ2 = ∥Y∥ψ2 = 1, uses E exp(X²) ≤ 2 and E exp(Y²) ≤ 2, and seeks E exp(|XY|) ≤ 2.

source_evidence.anchor: Proof of Lemma 2.7.7, two applications of Young’s inequality
source_evidence.observation: The proof uses |XY| ≤ X²/2 + Y²/2 and exp(X²/2) exp(Y²/2) ≤ (exp(X²) + exp(Y²))/2, yielding E exp(|XY|) ≤ 2 without using independence.

source_evidence.location: PDF page 16; printed page 27; and PDF page 22; printed page 33
source_evidence.observation: The relevant norm definitions are ∥Z∥ψ2 = inf {t > 0 : E exp(Z²/t²) ≤ 2} and ∥Z∥ψ1 = inf {t > 0 : E exp(|Z|/t) ≤ 2}.

binders: Jointly defined real-valued random variables X and Y.
definitions_and_conventions: The product XY is the pointwise product of the two random variables.
implicit_context: X and Y live on a common probability space so that the pointwise product XY is defined.
The source’s proof uses homogeneity to normalize both ψ2 norms to one and then rescales.

details: No independence hypothesis is stated or used; arbitrary dependence between X and Y is allowed.
The displayed norm inequality has exact multiplicative constant 1.
Neither X nor Y is assumed to have mean zero.
The argument uses the normalized quadratic exponential moments and deterministic Young inequalities, not factorization of expectations.

undebatable_constraints: Both X and Y must be sub-gaussian.
The conclusion includes both sub-exponentiality of XY and the ψ1 norm bound.
The right-hand side is the product ∥X∥ψ2 ∥Y∥ψ2 with exact constant 1.
No independence or mean-zero hypothesis may be added.
X and Y must be jointly situated so that XY is a random variable.
